Topic 01 — Measuring Athletic Performance

Low-Speed vs High-Speed Strength

Low-Speed Strength
Force a muscle/group exerts in one maximal effort.
Quantified by 1RM (bench, squat) or max isokinetic force.
No expensive equipment needed → most common max-strength test.
Why it matters1RM tests reflect the dynamic ability sport requires.
High-Speed Strength
Ability to exert high force at high contraction speed.
Also called (max) anaerobic power.
≈1 s duration → ATP-PCr is primary energy source.
Scores includePower clean/snatch 1RM, vertical jump height, stair-sprint time.
Topic 01 — Measuring Athletic Performance

High-Speed Power & Net Impulse

Jump Height = Net Impulse
Jump height is a function of force applied > bodyweight over time (net impulse) during ankle/knee/hip extension.
↑ net impulse (force × time) → ↑ takeoff velocity.
Interpretation trapAthlete gains body mass but jumps to the same height → same takeoff velocity on a heavier body = power output ↑, though jump height looks unchanged.
Force applied > bodyweight
→
Net impulse
→
Takeoff velocity
→
Jump height
Topic 01 — Measuring Athletic Performance

Load-Velocity Profile (VBT)

Velocity-Based Training
Bar speed ↓ linearly as load ↑ → individualized profile from loads at 20/40/60/80/90% 1RM.
Useful for prescribing/evaluating training intensity.
Don't use to predict 1RM. Estimates from a load-velocity profile are highly variable and consistently overestimate true 1RM — risking unsafe, mis-programmed loads. Test 1RM directly.
Topic 01 — Measuring Athletic Performance

Anaerobic Capacity & Muscular Endurance

Anaerobic Capacity
Max rate of energy production, phosphagen + glycolytic systems combined.
Quantified as max power output over 30–90 s.
(vs. anaerobic power tests: only a few seconds).
Local Muscular Endurance
Certain muscle(s) performing repeated contractions vs submaximal resistance.
Continuous, no rest, no extraneous movement.
e.g. max chin-ups, dips, push-ups, or reps at % 1RM.
Topic 01 — Measuring Athletic Performance

Aerobic Capacity

Aerobic Power
Max rate of energy production via oxidation of CHO/fat/protein.
Expressed as mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ (VO₂max).
Direct measurement uncommon in the field → estimated via performance tests.
  • Distance run1 mile (1.6 km) or more — time-based estimate
  • MAS testMaximal aerobic speed field protocol
  • Yo-Yo IRTIntermittent recovery — mimics team-sport demands
Topic 01 — Measuring Athletic Performance

Agility & Speed

Agility
Speed
Definition
Rapid whole-body change of direction/speed in response to a stimulus
Distance covered per unit time
Components
Change-of-direction speed + cognitive/perceptual factor
Acceleration (short) vs max velocity (longer sprint)
Test examples
T-test · 5-0-5 · 5-10-5 (pro agility) · L-drill
10 yd (accel) · 40 yd (max speed)
Hand-timed sprints run up to 0.24 s faster than electronic timing (tester reaction delay + anticipation). Prefer electronic timing gates + split times (10/20/40 yd) whenever available.
Topic 01 — Measuring Athletic Performance

Athletic Motor Skill Competency

AMSC (Lloyd et al.)
Foundational movement skills underpinning athletic movement in youth.
Screened via tools: FMS, tuck jump assessment (TJA), RTSB, back squat assessment.
Process-oriented assessmentIdentifies strength/mobility/neuromuscular deficits to guide programming.
Record on video for retrospective review. Best-repetition scoring (FMS, RTSB) vs sum-of-repetitions scoring (TJA) — the latter captures the movement variability youth show from ongoing brain maturation and growth spurts.
Topic 01 — Measuring Athletic Performance

Flexibility, Balance & Stability

Flexibility
Range of motion about a joint.
Goniometer (joint angle) or sit-and-reach box (low back/hip).
Move slowly into stretch, hold — no ballistic bouncing allowed.
Balance & Stability
Balance = maintaining COG over base of support.
Stability = returning to position after disturbance.
BESS and SEBT: strong reliability, well supported in literature.
Topic 01 — Measuring Athletic Performance

Body Composition & Anthropometry

Body Composition
Relative proportions of fat vs lean mass (2-component model).
Skinfold calipers: most valid/reliable field method (r = 0.99).
DXA = gold standard; bioimpedance/plethysmography also used.
Anthropometry
Height, weight, selected girths.
Stadiometer for height; certified balance scale for weight.
Weigh in the morning, minimal dry clothing, consistent hydration.
Topic 01 — Recap

Measuring Athletic Performance — Recap

✅
Strength & Power
Low-speed (1RM) vs high-speed (jump/power) — net impulse drives jump height.
✅
Capacity & Endurance
Anaerobic (30–90 s), local muscular endurance, aerobic (VO₂max).
✅
Agility, Speed & Movement
COD + cognition; electronic timing preferred; AMSC for youth screening.
✅
Flexibility, Balance, Body Comp
Static stretch only; BESS/SEBT for balance; skinfolds for body fat.

Every physical quality needs its own valid, reliable test — choosing the right measurement is the first step in performance testing.

Topic 02 — Protocols, Procedures & Equipment

Three Layers of a Testing System

Protocols
Systematic plan for achieving specific objectives.
Overarching strategy: test types + frequency across the season.
Procedures
Detailed step-by-step instructions within the protocol framework.
Ensures consistent data collection (e.g. vertical jump steps).
Equipment
Tools/technology required to implement tests.
Selection must fit the specific athletic environment.
Topic 02 — Protocols, Procedures & Equipment

AI & Machine Learning in Testing

AI in Athlete Testing
AI = a computer performing tasks associated with intelligent beings — reason, discover meaning, generalize, learn.
ML = machines learning from data without explicit human input.
ApplicationsBiomechanical/movement analysis, phone-based jump/speed/velocity tests, injury-prediction models.
"Garbage in, garbage out" — model quality depends entirely on data quantity and quality. Scrutinize the accuracy/validity of any AI-driven tool before trusting it.
Topic 02 — Protocols, Procedures & Equipment

Choosing Equipment

1
Would the information provided be helpful?
2
Can you trust the information provided?
3
Can you integrate, manage, and analyze the data effectively?
4
Can you implement the technology in your practice?
Before adopting any testing technology, confirm its validity/reliability, ease of use, and relevance to the athlete's sport.

Max Muscular Strength (Low-Speed Strength)

1RM Tests

1RM Bench Press
EquipmentBarbell, plates, 2 safety locks (5 lb gradations); sturdy bench with integral rack (adjustable height preferred).
PersonnelOne spotter, one recorder.
1. Warm up 5–10 reps light-moderate load.
2. 2+ heavier warm-up sets of 2–5 reps.
3. Measure 1RM within 3–5 attempts post warm-up.
1RM Bench Pull
EquipmentBarbell, plates, 2 safety locks; high flat bench (e.g. seal row bench).
PersonnelOne spotter, one recorder.
1. Closed pronated grip, wider than shoulder width, from the hang position.
2. Pull bar to lower chest/upper abdomen, elbows up; feet stay off the ground.
3. Valid rep = bar touches bench, lowered under control to full elbow extension.
1RM Back Squat
EquipmentBarbell, plates, 2 safety locks; squat rack with adjustable spotting bars; flat, solid surface.
PersonnelTwo spotters, one recorder.
1. Warm-up as per bench press.
2. Load increments are larger than bench press.
3. Measure 1RM within 3–5 attempts.
Max Muscular Power (High-Speed Strength) · Test 4 of 13

Isometric Mid-Thigh Pull (IMTP)

Equipment
Force plate(s) ≥1,000 Hz (or strain gauge/crane scale, 100–133 Hz); immovable fixed bar with stepwise height adjustment; weightlifting straps; computer/tablet with force-time software; goniometer.
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Set rack height so the bar mirrors the weightlifting "2nd pull" position — across the upper thigh, immediately inferior to the pelvis.
2
Upright trunk, feet hip-width apart, slight knee flex, clean grip + straps; knee ≈120–145°, hip ≈125–150° (varies with anthropometrics).
3
Complete 1–3 familiarization sessions, then a dynamic warm-up + submax trials at 50/70/90% intensity, 1–2 min rest.
4
Perform ≥3 max-effort trials, 1–2 min rest; 3–5 s trials for peak force, ≤1 s if RFD is the focus.
5
Discard a trial for pre-tension, a countermovement, an unquiet 1 s standing period (>50 N change), or if peak force varies >15% between trials.
Key metrics: peak force and force at 50/100/150/200/250 ms. RFD (peak: 20 ms window) and impulse are quantified over 0–50/0–100/0–200/0–250 ms windows, reported in absolute and relative (per kg) terms.
Max Muscular Power (High-Speed Strength) · Test 5 of 13

Nordic Hamstring Test

Equipment
Commercially available instrumented device for eccentric hamstring strength (or a video recording device); stable flooring surface.
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Kneel on the device, ankles under the hooks (contact only with the back of the ankles, no pushing off with the toes); knees at 90°; avoid flexing forward at the hips.
2
Lean forward under control, extending the knees, keeping a straight line from knees through shoulders.
3
Use the hands to push back up to start; typically 3–6 sets.
4
Instrumented: record absolute eccentric force (N), with optional ratio/allometric scaling, torque (Nm), or L/R asymmetry %.
Video-only: report the break-point angle — where the athlete loses active control of the descent — as a moderate proxy for eccentric hamstring strength.
Max Muscular Power (High-Speed Strength) · Test 6 of 13

1RM Power Clean

Equipment
Olympic-style barbell with revolving sleeve, plates, 2 safety locks (5 lb gradations); lifting platform or designated area.
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Instruct the athlete in proper power clean technique.
2
Warm-up sets performed and load increments selected as for the 1RM bench press.
3
Measure 1RM within 3–5 attempts.
Because the power clean has high technical demands, two athletes with the same muscular power capacity can differ greatly in tested 1RM — lessening its value for predicting athletic performance.
Max Muscular Power (High-Speed Strength) · Test 7 of 13

Standing Long (Broad) Jump

Equipment
Flat jumping area ≥20 ft (6 m); tape measure ≥10 ft (3 m); duct/masking tape (or a premarked jumping mat in 0.5 in/1 cm increments).
Personnel
One distance judge, one recorder.
Steps
1
Place a 2–3 ft length of tape as the starting line; athlete stands with toes just behind it.
2
Athlete performs a countermovement and jumps forward as far as possible.
3
Must land on the feet to score, otherwise repeat the trial.
4
Mark the rearmost heel; measure the distance from the starting line.
5
Best of 3 trials, nearest 0.5 in / 1 cm.
Max Muscular Power (High-Speed Strength) · Test 8 of 13

Vertical Jump — Force Plate

Equipment
Force plate on a stable surface; computer, tablet, or phone with corresponding software.
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Calibrate and set up the force plate per manufacturer instructions, ideally in the same location each time; zero it with nothing on the plate immediately before testing.
2
Without a preparatory/stutter step, the athlete performs a countermovement — quickly flexing the knees and hips, moving the trunk forward/downward, swinging the arms back.
3
Hands fixed on the hips throughout takeoff is standard; jumping with an arm swing (Abalakov) can also be tested — track which method was used and stay consistent.
Jump height from force plates/contact mats is measured as center-of-mass rise above its height at takeoff — not standing height — so it isn't directly comparable to jump-and-reach scores.
Max Muscular Power (High-Speed Strength) · Test 8 of 13

Vertical Jump — Wall & Chalk

Equipment
Smooth wall with a ceiling higher than the highest expected jump; chalk in a color different from the wall.
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Chalk the fingertips of the athlete's dominant hand.
2
Standing with the dominant shoulder ~6 in (15 cm) from the wall, both feet flat, reach as high as possible and mark the wall.
3
Lower the hand, then without a preparatory/stutter step perform a countermovement jump; the dominant arm reaches upward, the nondominant arm moves downward.
4
At peak height, swipe a second chalk mark with the dominant hand's fingers; score = vertical distance between the two marks.
5
Best of 3 trials, nearest 0.5 in / 1.0 cm.
Max Muscular Power (High-Speed Strength) · Test 8 of 13

Vertical Jump — Vertec Device

Equipment
Commercial device with a stack of movable, color-coded horizontal vanes.
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Adjust the vane stack within standing reach; the highest vane pushed forward flat-footed sets the standing touch height.
2
Raise the vane stack by an estimated jump-height distance so the athlete lands within the set of vanes (correct on the second attempt if needed).
3
Without a preparatory/stutter step, perform a countermovement jump — dominant arm reaching upward, nondominant arm moving downward.
4
At peak height, tap the highest possible vane with the dominant hand's fingers.
5
Best of 3 trials, nearest 0.5 in / 1 cm (the distance between adjacent vanes).
Sources of error: a lag between hand contact and true center-of-mass peak, and shoulder mobility limiting reach height.
Max Muscular Power (High-Speed Strength) · Test 9 of 13

Squat Jump (Static Vertical Jump)

Equipment
Same as the vertical jump (force plate, or a switch/contact mat — estimates jump height but can't measure force).
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Procedure is the same as the vertical jump, but the countermovement is removed.
2
Athlete descends into a squat (knee angle ≈110°), holds for 2–3 s, then jumps vertically with hands fixed on the hips.
3
Takeoff/landing/jump strategy stay consistent across trials — confirm no countermovement dip visually or via the force-time curve.
4
Best of 3 trials recorded.
CMJ height ÷ squat jump height = eccentric utilization ratio.
Max Muscular Power (High-Speed Strength) · Test 10 of 13

Drop Jump

Equipment
Box, 8–16 in (20–40 cm) height; floor with good traction; force plates, switch mats, optoelectronic systems, or smartphone apps.
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Step out (don't jump or step down) and free-fall from as close as possible to box height; typical heights: 20/30/40 cm (8/12/16 in) — higher box = greater plyometric demand.
2
Land, then jump again as quickly as possible, aiming for a short ground contact time via high leg stiffness (limited ankle/knee/hip flexion) while still jumping as high as possible.
3
Perform at least 2–3 sets.
Reported variables: jump height (flight time), ground contact time, and reactive strength index (jump height ÷ ground contact time).
Max Muscular Power (High-Speed Strength) · Test 11 of 13

Rebound Jump

Equipment
Floor with good traction; force plates, jump mats, optoelectronic systems, or smartphone apps.
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Perform a maximal countermovement jump, followed by a set number of rebound jumps or a set duration (e.g. 10 s).
2
Aim for a short ground contact time via high leg stiffness while still jumping as high as possible.
Reported variables: jump height, ground contact time, reactive strength index. The 10-5 repeated jump test uses 10 maximal rebound jumps after the initial CMJ; the best 5 reps by reactive strength index are averaged for the score.
Max Muscular Power (High-Speed Strength) · Test 12 of 13

Margaria-Kalamen Test

Equipment
Staircase, 9+ steps (~7 in/18 cm each), flat lead-up ≥20 ft (6 m); measuring tape/stick; electronic timer with start/stop switches; scale.
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Measure step height; calculate elevation from the 3rd to 9th step (6 × step height).
2
Place the timer's start switch on the 3rd step, stop switch on the 9th step.
3
Weigh, warm up, and let the athlete practice running the stairs 3 at a time.
4
Sprint from 20 ft (6 m), then up the stairs 3 at a time (3rd → 6th → 9th step) as fast as possible.
5
Time from 3rd- to 9th-step contact, nearest 0.01 s; repeat twice more with 2–3 min rest.
Power (W) = (weight in N × height in m) ÷ time (s) — height = elevation from the 3rd to 9th step.
Max Muscular Power (High-Speed Strength) · Test 13 of 13

Velocity-Based Testing (VBT)

Equipment
Commercial VBT device (IMU, linear position transducer, depth-sensing camera, or computer-vision smartphone app) + Olympic barbell/plates/collars for the chosen lift (e.g. 1RM back squat).
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Position the device per its type — transducer under/tethered to the bar, IMU affixed directly to the bar.
2
Select the exercise (bench press, squat, deadlift) based on the athlete/sport/session.
3
Record bar velocity (m/s), power (W), and peak force (N) from the device — metrics vary by device.
VBT data can be used to build a load-velocity profile, but don't use it to predict 1RM.
Anaerobic Capacity · Test 14 of 15

300-Yard (274 m) Shuttle Run

Equipment
Stopwatch (≥0.1 s resolution); two parallel lines 25 yd (23 m) apart.
Personnel
One timer, two line judges.
Steps
1
Pair athletes of similar ability; position two behind one line, facing the other.
2
On signal, sprint to the far line (25 yd), make foot contact, sprint back — 6 round trips total (6 × 50 yd = 300 yd/274 m), as fast as possible without stopping.
3
Record time to the nearest 0.1 s; rest 5 min.
4
Repeat for a second trial; average the two trials to the nearest 0.1 s.
Anaerobic Capacity · Test 15 of 15

90-Second Box Jump Test

Equipment
Stopwatch; box 18 in (46 cm) high × 30 in (76 cm) wide; nonslip surface.
Personnel
One recorder/tester.
Steps
1
Starting on top of the box, jump down laterally to one side, then back up to the top; repeat to the opposite side. Each top-of-box arrival = 1 rep.
2
Leave the ground with two feet and land on top with two feet each time — no stepping up.
3
Continue for 90 s; record reps performed with proper form.
Local Muscular Endurance · Test 16 of 19

Partial Curl-Up

Equipment
Metronome; ruler; masking tape; mat.
Personnel
One recorder/technique judge.
Steps
1
Supine on a mat, knees at 90°, arms at the sides with fingers touching a 4 in (10 cm) tape marker; a second tape marker sits parallel at 4.7 in (12 cm, under age 45) or 3.1 in (8 cm, 45+).
2
Set metronome to 40 beats/min (20 curl-ups/min); curl up to lift the shoulder blades off the mat (trunk at 30°) in time with the beat — upper back must touch down between reps; avoid flexing the neck.
3
Perform as many curl-ups as possible without pausing, to a maximum of 75.
Local Muscular Endurance · Test 17 of 19

Push-Up

Equipment
4 in (10 cm) diameter foam roller (for the modified version).
Personnel
One recorder/technique judge.
Steps
1
Standard: hands shoulder-width apart, elbows/body straight; bottom position = chest contacts the recorder's vertically held fist.
2
Modified: start on the knees (flexed 90°, ankles crossed) instead of the feet; torso contacts a foam roller at the bottom instead of a fist.
3
Reps that don't reach the bottom position aren't counted.
Local Muscular Endurance · Test 18 of 19

Army Fitness Test (AFT)
Hand-Release Push-Up (HRP)

Equipment
Level, nonslip ground/flooring surface.
Personnel
One recorder/technique judge.
Steps
1
Prone start — chest, hips, legs on the ground, hands flat with index fingers inside the shoulders, feet ≤1 boot-width apart.
2
On "Go," perform as many push-ups as possible in 2 min, keeping a straight line from ankles to head — no flexing the knees/hips or lifting the feet.
3
At the bottom, either lift both hands to create visible space (hand-lift variant) or fully extend the arms to 90° from the torso (arm-extension variant) before the next rep.
4
Rest only in the front-rest (top push-up) position; test ends if motionless >5 s, a foot lifts, or a knee touches down.
Local Muscular Endurance · Test 19 of 19

YMCA Bench Press Test

Equipment
Barbell, plates, 2 safety locks totaling 80 lb (36 kg) for males or 35 lb (16 kg) for females; flat bench (preferably with an upright rack); metronome.
Personnel
One spotter/recorder.
Steps
1
Warm up with 5–10 reps at a light-moderate load.
2
Load 80 lb (men) / 35 lb (women); set metronome to 60 beats/min (30 reps/min — one beat up, one beat down).
3
Lift off the rack, extend the elbows, then lower to the chest and press to full extension in time with the metronome until the athlete can no longer keep pace.
Aerobic Capacity · Test 20 of 24

1.5-Mile (2.4 km) Run

Equipment
Stopwatch; quarter-mile track or a measured/marked 1.5-mile (2.4 km) flat course.
Personnel
One tester to call times, one recorder.
Steps
1
Warm up and stretch; make each athlete identifiable at the finish (numbers pinned if needed).
2
Line up behind the start; on signal, run the distance at the fastest steady pace they can maintain.
3
Record each athlete's time in minutes and seconds as they cross the finish.
Aerobic Capacity · Test 21 of 24

12-Minute Run

Equipment
400 m (437 yd) track or flat looped course marked every 100 m; stopwatch.
Personnel
One tester to call positions, one recorder.
Steps
1
Line up at the start; on signal, cover as much distance as possible in 12 min (running, or walking if necessary).
2
On signal at 12 min, all athletes stop in place.
3
Calculate distance (laps × 400 m — e.g. 5.25 laps × 400 m = 2,100 m).
Aerobic Capacity · Test 22 of 24

Yo-Yo Intermittent Recovery Test

Equipment
Cones; tape measure ≥30 m (33 yd); Yo-Yo IRT1 audio software; wireless speakers; recording sheet; flat floor with good traction.
Personnel
One tester/recorder, one spotter.
Steps
1
Set up a 20 m (22 yd) course with markers 2 m (7 ft) apart at each end, plus a 5 m (16 ft) mark behind the start line.
2
Warm up with a submaximal practice run.
3
On signal, run to the turning line and back in time with the beeps; after the start marker, jog to the 5 m mark and back before the next signal.
4
One foot must be on/over the start or turning line at each beep; speed increases progressively.
5
Test ends when the athlete can't hold pace for 2 consecutive intervals (a warning is given on the first miss); record the final level and interval count.
IRT1 starts at 10 km/h (6.2 mph); IRT2 starts at 13 km/h (8.1 mph) — IRT1 is the recommended version for most testing.
Aerobic Capacity · Test 23 of 24

Maximal Aerobic Speed Test

Equipment
Cones; tape measure ≥30 m (33 yd); test-specific audio software; wireless speakers; recording sheet; indoor/outdoor track ≥200 m (219 yd).
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Place cones every 25 m (27 yd) around the track.
2
Start at 8–12 km/h (5–7 mph), typically 10 km/h (6 mph); increase by 1 km/h (0.6 mph) every 2 min until the athlete can't maintain the pace.
3
The last speed held for ≥2 min = the speed associated with VO2max (MAS); terminate if the athlete misses a cone on 2 consecutive occasions.
4
Add 0.5 km/h if the athlete completes a half stage; VO2max ≈ 3.5 × MAS (km/h).
Without audio, whistles can be timed manually — e.g. every 9 s for 10 km/h with 25 m cone spacing.
Aerobic Capacity · Test 24 of 24

30-15 Intermittent
Fitness Test (IFT)

Equipment
40 m (44 yd) stable running surface; measuring tape; marking cones; 30-15 IFT audio recording + player.
Personnel
One recorder/tester.
Steps
1
Set up cones at lines A, B, C; warm up with a submaximal practice run.
2
Start at line A; first interval at 8.0 km/h (5 mph), increasing 0.5 km/h (0.3 mph) each stage.
3
Run between lines A and C, passing each 3 m (10 ft) zone at lines A/B/C in time with the beeps.
4
A different beep signals 15 s of recovery (walk to the next line) before the next interval.
5
Advance until failing to reach the line on 3 consecutive beeps; record the final stage speed (Vmax), corrected by 0.7 s per change of direction.
Change of Direction or Agility · Test 25 of 29

T-Test

Equipment
Four cones; tape measure ≥5 yd (4.6 m); stopwatch or timing gates; flat floor with good traction.
Personnel
One tester/recorder, one spotter.
Steps
1
Arrange 4 cones (A, B, C, D); set timing gates at start/finish.
2
From point A, sprint forward to B and touch its base with the right hand.
3
Shuffle left 5 yd to C (touch with left hand), then right 10 yd to D (touch with right hand), then left 5 yd back to B (touch with left hand) — face forward throughout, no crossing feet.
4
Backpedal past A to finish; best of 2 trials, nearest 0.1 s.
Disqualified for missing a cone touch, crossing the feet instead of shuffling, or not facing forward throughout.
Change of Direction or Agility · Test 26 of 29

Hexagon Test

Equipment
Adhesive tape (contrasting color); measuring tape/stick; stopwatch; flat floor with good traction.
Personnel
One timer/recorder, one line judge.
Steps
1
Tape a hexagon on the floor, 24 in (61 cm) sides at 120° angles; athlete starts centered, facing one direction throughout.
2
On signal, double-leg hop from center over each side and back, clockwise, until all 6 sides are covered 3 times (18 jumps total), ending back at center.
3
Landing on a side, losing balance, or changing facing direction stops and restarts the trial (after full recovery).
4
Best of 3 trials, nearest 0.1 s.
Change of Direction or Agility · Test 27 of 29

5-10-5 Test

Equipment
Field marked with 3 parallel lines 5 yd (4.6 m) apart; stopwatch or timing gates.
Personnel
One timer/recorder, one line judge.
Steps
1
Set timing gates at start/finish (and each turn line, if available, for splits).
2
Straddle the center line in a 3-point stance.
3
On signal, sprint 5 yd left, change direction and sprint 10 yd right, change direction and sprint 5 yd back to center — hand/foot contact required at every line, kept consistent across trials.
4
Best of 2 trials, nearest 0.01 s.
Also called the pro agility test or the 20-yard shuttle.
Change of Direction or Agility · Test 28 of 29

5-0-5 Test

Equipment
Seven cones; stopwatch or timing gates.
Personnel
One timer/recorder, one line judge.
Steps
1
Arrange cones and, if available, timing lights per the course layout; warm up with a practice run.
2
From the start line, sprint 10 m (11 yd) through the first timing gate, then 5 m (5 yd) further to the turning line (one foot on/over it), turn and accelerate off.
3
Only slow down after passing back through the timing gate a second time.
4
Best of 2 trials, nearest 0.1 s; test the preferred leg, or ≥2 trials each leg if testing both.
Change of Direction or Agility · Test 29 of 29

Illinois Test

Equipment
Stopwatch or timing lights; tape measure; 8 cones.
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Set a 10 m × 5 m (11 × 5 yd) course: 4 cones at the corners, 4 more centered along the 5 m width — creating 3 aisles of 2/4/2 cones.
2
Athlete lies prone at the outside-left cone; on "Go," sprints 10 m ahead, turns, and sprints back to the middle aisle.
3
Slalom through the 4 center cones in both directions, then run to the cone at the far end of the third aisle.
4
Sprint the final 10 m aisle to finish; timer stops on completion.
Speed · Test 30 of 30

Straight-Line Sprint Tests

Equipment
Stopwatch or timing gates; flat running surface with start/finish lines a set distance apart (e.g. 40 yd/37 m; 10/20/40 m), ≥20 yd (18 m) of deceleration space after the finish; multiple gates optional for splits.
Personnel
One timer/recorder.
Steps
1
Warm up and dynamically stretch; allow ≥2 submax practice runs.
2
3- or 4-point starting stance.
3
On signal, sprint the set distance at maximal speed.
4
Best split times of 2 trials, nearest 0.1 s; ≥2 min active recovery between trials.
Multiple gates (e.g. start/10 yd/20 yd/40 yd finish) give extra insight into acceleration capacity, not just maximal speed.
Balance and Stability · Test 31 of 32

Balance Error Scoring
System (BESS)

Equipment
Foam balance pad; stopwatch.
Personnel
One timer/recorder.
Steps
1
Three stances: double-leg (feet together), single-leg (nondominant foot, contralateral leg ~90° flexed), and tandem (dominant foot in front) — each on a firm surface and a soft surface.
2
Hold each stance 20 s, eyes closed, hands on hips; try to regain position quickly if balance is lost.
3
Errors: opening the eyes, lifting hands off hips, touchdown of the non-stance foot, a step/hop/other foot movement, lifting the forefoot/heel, >30° hip flexion/abduction, or being out of position >5 s.
4
Sum all errors into a single score.
Balance and Stability · Test 32 of 32

Star Excursion
Balance Test (SEBT)

Equipment
Adhesive tape.
Personnel
One recorder.
Steps
1
Stand centered on an 8-line grid (lines 120 cm/47 in, at 45° increments).
2
Single-leg stance, reach with the other leg to touch as far as possible along each line, then return to bilateral stance — same facing direction and stance leg throughout a trial.
3
Measure distance from center to the touch point; starting direction/support leg chosen randomly, 3 trials per condition, averaged, with 15 s rest between reaches.
4
Discard a trial if the athlete misses the line, lifts the stance foot, loses balance, or can't hold start/return for 1 full second; give ≥4 practice trials first.
Testing just the anteromedial, medial, and posteromedial directions is sufficient for most situations.
Flexibility · Test 33 of 34

Sit-and-Reach Test

Equipment
Measuring tape/stick; adhesive tape (or a standard sit-and-reach box).
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Tape the measuring stick to the floor with a crossbar of tape at the 15 in (38 cm) mark.
2
Warm up the hamstrings/low back with nonballistic movement (e.g. 3–5 min brisk walking, standing toe reaches, jogging in place).
3
Sit shoeless, stick between the legs, feet 12 in (30 cm) apart, heels near the 15 in mark.
4
Reach forward slowly with both hands, hold momentarily, exhale and drop the head between the arms; keep hands level, fingertips on the stick.
5
Best of 3 trials, nearest 0.25 in / 1 cm.
Stay consistent with the device used (tape/stick vs box) across repeat testing of the same athlete.
Flexibility · Test 34 of 34

Overhead Squat

Equipment
Wooden dowel or barbell.
Personnel
One tester/recorder.
Steps
1
Hold the dowel overhead, shoulders fully flexed, elbows locked; grip = 2× biacromial width; feet shoulder-width, toes forward or slightly out.
2
Squat by flexing the hips and knees first, heels staying down throughout.
3
Lower until the hip crease is below the top of the knee, torso upright, dowel comfortably overhead.
4
Perform ≥5 reps, viewed from the side; score qualitatively as pass/fail.
Warm up and familiarize the athlete with the movement pattern first to protect test validity.
Body Composition · Test 35 of 36

Skinfold Measurements

Equipment
Skinfold calipers; flexible tape measure; marking pen.
Personnel
One tester, one recorder.
Steps
1
Measure on dry skin, before exercise; select sites/equations based on the population tested.
2
Grasp a fold of skin + subcutaneous fat; place caliper prongs perpendicular to the fold, 0.5–1 in (1–2 cm) from the fingers.
3
Release the caliper's spring tension; read the dial 1–2 s later, to the nearest 0.5 mm.
4
Take a second measurement at each site; if the two agree within 10%, average them — otherwise take more readings until two agree, then average.
Minimum SEE for population-specific skinfold equations is ±3–5% — e.g. a 24% body-fat reading carries at least a 6% range (21–27%).
Body Composition · Test 36 of 36

Bioelectrical Impedance (BIA)

Equipment
BIA device.
Personnel
One recorder.
Steps
1
Program the device with the athlete's sex, weight, and height.
2
Have the athlete hold the electrodes or stand barefoot on them, per the device type.
3
Press start and wait the device's specified duration (usually under 5 s).
4
Record the body composition measurements provided.
For consistent tracking, test first thing in the morning, before exercise, food, or water, and after voiding.
Anthropometry · Test 37 of 37

Girth Measurements

Equipment
Flexible, spring-loaded tape measure (e.g. a Gulick tape).
Personnel
One tester, one recorder.
Steps
1
Position the athlete in a relaxed anatomical position for each site.
2
Chest — nipple level (males) or maximum circumference above the breasts (females).
3
Right upper arm & forearm — at maximal circumference, elbow fully extended, palm up, arm abducted to parallel with the floor.
4
Waist (umbilicus level), hips (maximal buttock protrusion, heels together), right thigh (max circumference, just below the buttocks), right calf (max circumference between knee and ankle).

Topic 04

Statistical
Evaluation of
Test Data

Turning raw scores into meaningful, comparable, and defensible numbers.

Topic 04 — Statistical Evaluation

Why Analyze Test Data?

1
Track change in performance over the training period.
2
Compare an individual/group to similarly tested groups.
3
Relate an athlete's score to the rest of the group.
4
Compare scores to local, state, national, or international norms.
Two traps when judging improvement alone: higher-status athletes improve less (diminishing returns), and athletes may sandbag the pretest to inflate "improvement." Insist on maximal effort at both ends.
Topic 04 — Statistical Evaluation

Types of Statistics

Descriptive
Summarizes/describes a whole known population.
Central tendency, variability, percentile rank.
Inferential
Draws conclusions about a population from a sample.
Assumes the sample truly represents the population.
Magnitude
Interprets the practical/clinical significance of change.
Smallest worthwhile change, effect size.
Topic 04 — Statistical Evaluation

Central Tendency

Mean
Sum of scores ÷ number of scores.
Most commonly used measure.
Median
Middle score when ranked.
Resists distortion from extreme scores.
Mode
Most frequent score.
Regarded as least useful measure.
Topic 04 — Statistical Evaluation

Variability

Range
Lowest score to highest score.
Simple, but ignores everything in between.
Standard Deviation
Dispersion of scores about the mean.
Small SD = tightly clustered; large SD = spread out.
Standard Deviation (Sample)
SD = √[Σ(x − x̄)² / (n − 1)]
x
Individual score
x̄
Mean of the scores
n
Sample size
Topic 04 — Statistical Evaluation

The Z-Score

Standardized Score
z = (x − x̄) / SD
x
Athlete's score
x̄
Group mean
SD
Group standard deviation
Worked example: 40-yd sprint = 4.6 s. Group mean = 5.00 s, SD = 0.33 s. z = (4.6 − 5.00) / 0.33 = −1.2 → 1.2 SD below (faster than) the group mean.
Plotting z-scores across multiple tests (strength, jump, agility, sprint, flexibility, body fat) visually flags which quality to prioritize in programming.
Topic 04 — Statistical Evaluation

Percentile Rank

Percentile Rank
% of test-takers scoring below a given individual.
Scores are ordered lowest → highest, same logic as the median.
Example75th percentile → 75% of the group scored below that athlete.
Topic 04 — Statistical Evaluation

Magnitude Statistics — SWC

Smallest Worthwhile Change
Smallest practically important change a test can detect.
Typically = 0.2 × between-subjects SD.
ExampleVertical jump SD = 10 cm in a female group → SWC = 0.2 × 10 = 2 cm.
Topic 04 — Statistical Evaluation

Magnitude Statistics — Effect Size

Effect Size
ES = (x̄ post − x̄ pre) / SD pre
x̄ post
Mean score after training
x̄ pre
Mean score before training
SD pre
Pretest standard deviation
Example: Bench 1RM pre = 104.5 kg (SD 5.7). Post (12 wk) = 111.7 kg. ES = (111.7 − 104.5) / 5.7 = 1.26 → interpreted as a large training effect.
SmallModerateLargeVery Large
0.20.61.22.0
Topic 04 — Recap

Statistical Evaluation — Recap

✅
Descriptive Stats
Mean, median, mode + range, SD, percentile rank.
✅
Z-Score
Standardizes a score in SD units from the mean.
✅
Inferential vs Magnitude
Population inference vs practical/clinical significance.
✅
SWC & Effect Size
0.2×SD and (post−pre)/SD-pre — small 0.2 to very large 2.0.

Numbers only become useful once you know how much change actually matters for that athlete, in that sport.

Topic 05

Developing
an Athletic
Profile

Combining test results into a picture of an athlete's sport-specific readiness.

Topic 05 — Developing an Athletic Profile

What Is an Athletic Profile?

Athletic Profile
Test results tied to the sport-specific abilities that matter for performance in a sport or position.
Built by combining selected test results, not any single score.
Topic 05 — Developing an Athletic Profile

The 6-Step Process

1
Select tests measuring parameters tied to the sport's physical demands.
2
Choose valid/reliable tests; sequence the battery with sufficient rest.
3
Administer the battery to as many athletes as possible.
4
Determine smallest worthwhile change; compare to norms where available.
5
Repeat testing (pre/post) and visualize the profile.
6
Use results to identify strengths/weaknesses and guide programming.
Topic 05 — Developing an Athletic Profile

Applied Example — Wrestling

Building a Wrestling Battery
Sport demands pulling strength, pushing strength, local muscular endurance.
Battery: max-rep push-ups + max-rep sit-ups.
Sequencing ruleSeparate the two tests by ≥10 min rest to allow recovery and protect score accuracy.
Coaches should store testing results over time and build their own norms once procedures are standardized.
